text:
17 modules later — what I've learned building a digital literacy platform for seniors.

When we started the Digital Confidence Centre, I thought the hard part would be the content.

It wasn't.

The hard part was unlearning every assumption I had about how people engage with technology.

Here's what 17 modules of building taught me:

1. Jargon is the enemy. Not complexity — jargon. Seniors understand complexity just fine. They've managed mortgages, raised children, run businesses. What stops them is language that assumes they already know.

2. Fear is the UX problem. Every design decision has to answer one question first: does this make someone feel safer or more anxious? If it's the latter, redesign it.

3. Progress matters more than completion. Seniors don't need to finish a module — they need to feel like they moved forward. That's a different goal, and it changes everything about how you structure content.

4. Celebrate the small wins out loud. That moment when someone realises they already knew how to do something — that's the moment confidence is born. Build for that.

5. The best teacher isn't the smartest person in the room. It's the most patient one.

We're at 17 modules and counting. Every one of them taught us something new about what it means to genuinely help someone feel capable in a world that keeps changing.

What have you learned from your users that surprised you?
image_prompt: Warm overhead photo of an older adult's hands holding a tablet, coffee cup nearby, soft natural light through a window

text:
The most common tech mistake seniors make — and it's not what you think.

Everyone assumes the answer is passwords, or clicking the wrong link, or falling for a scam.

Those are real issues. But they're not the most common mistake.

The most common mistake is giving up too soon.

Not because seniors lack intelligence or curiosity. But because the moment something goes wrong — an unexpected pop-up, a button that disappears, a page that loads differently than last time — the internal voice kicks in:

"I'm not good at this."
"I was never a tech person."
"I'll just ask my grandson."

And then they stop.

The mistake isn't a click. It's a conclusion — drawn too quickly, reinforced too often — that technology isn't for them.

Our job at the Digital Confidence Centre isn't to teach people how to use apps. It's to interrupt that voice long enough that they can discover they already have most of the skills they need.

Confidence is the product. The modules are just the delivery mechanism.

If you work in tech — whether that's product, support, design, or development — ask yourself: what are we doing that accidentally confirms that voice?

And what could we do differently?
image_prompt: A senior woman looking slightly frustrated at a tablet, then a second frame showing her smiling — conveying the journey from confusion to confidence

text:
Why we built the Digital Confidence Centre bilingual from day one.

Short answer: because the Francophone seniors in Ontario deserve the same experience as everyone else. Not a translation. An experience.

Longer answer:

When we made the decision to build bilingually, we weren't just adding a language toggle. We were committing to a different way of thinking about who this platform is for.

Translation is about words. Localisation is about people.

A well-localised French version doesn't just replace English words with French ones. It considers:

— How trust is built differently in Francophone communities
— Which government resources and support lines are French-language accessible
— The specific phrasing that an older adult from Northern Ontario would actually use
— The rhythm of a sentence that feels natural to read at 72, not just grammatically correct

We're a small team. Building bilingually costs us more time and more money.

We did it anyway.

Because digital literacy isn't a privilege for English speakers. And if we were serious about reaching the seniors who need this most — not just the ones who are easiest to reach — bilingual wasn't optional.

It was the baseline.

If you're building anything for public benefit in Canada, ask yourself: who are you leaving out by defaulting to English only?
image_prompt: Split-screen showing the same DCC screen in English and French, clean and welcoming design visible on both sides

text:
What Brenda taught me about user experience.

Brenda is 74. She lives in St. Thomas, Ontario. She has an iPad her daughter bought her two Christmases ago.

She used it mostly for photos until she found our platform.

The first time Brenda went through Module 1, she stopped halfway through and called her daughter.

"There's something on the internet that's teaching me things and it actually makes sense."

That call changed how I think about UX.

Because Brenda wasn't saying the design was clever. She wasn't praising the navigation or the colour choices or the font size controls.

She was saying: someone thought about me.

That's the bar. Not delight — consideration. Not innovation — respect.

Every senior who opens a digital product has had some experience — usually many — where they felt like an afterthought. Where the design assumed a level of familiarity they didn't have. Where the error message told them what went wrong but not what to do next.

When you get it right, they don't describe the features. They describe how it made them feel.

Brenda is fictional. But she's based on hundreds of real conversations.

Every product team should have a Brenda on their wall. Not as a demographic. As a reminder.

Who are you actually building for?
image_prompt: Warm portrait-style photo of an older woman smiling at a tablet, natural home setting, genuinely warm expression — not staged

text:
The 3-Second Rule we teach every senior learner.

It's one of the simplest things in the Digital Confidence Centre. And it might be the most useful.

Before you tap, click, or respond to anything unexpected — wait 3 seconds.

That's it. That's the rule.

Here's why it works:

Most online scams and mistakes rely on urgency. They need you to act before you think. A message that says "Your account will be closed in 5 minutes" is designed to bypass the part of your brain that evaluates risk.

Three seconds is enough to let that part catch up.

In those 3 seconds, ask yourself:
— Did I expect this?
— Does this make sense?
— Would the real company really contact me this way?

More often than not, those three questions reveal the answer.

We've taught this to seniors in workshops across Ontario. The feedback is always the same:

"I wish someone had told me this years ago."

Simplicity is underrated in digital safety education. We keep trying to build smarter tools when sometimes what people need is a pause.

Share this with someone who could use it. The 3-Second Rule costs nothing and prevents a lot.
image_prompt: Bold graphic with the text '3 Second Rule' in large type, simple blue background, clean and easy to read — shareable infographic style

text:
Why we include a 'getting unstuck' module before we teach anything else.

Most digital literacy programs start with the same thing: here's how to use the device.

We start somewhere different: here's what to do when something goes wrong.

That choice is deliberate.

Because the single biggest barrier to senior tech adoption isn't lack of knowledge. It's fear of getting stuck.

When you're learning something new, mistakes feel catastrophic if you don't have a recovery plan. But if you know — before you even start — that there are three simple things you can always do to get back on track, everything changes.

Our 'Escape Hatch' module teaches exactly that:
1. Go back to the home screen
2. Close the app and reopen it
3. Ask for help without embarrassment

None of those are technically complicated. But knowing them ahead of time gives learners a safety net. And with a safety net, they're willing to try.

Willingness to try is where learning begins.

If you design training programs, onboarding flows, or educational content — think about what you're teaching people to do when it goes wrong. That module might matter more than all the others.

What's your 'getting unstuck' strategy?
image_prompt: Simple diagram showing three recovery steps with arrows, clean educational graphic style, warm blue tones

text:
The biggest barrier to senior tech adoption isn't skill. It's confidence.

I want to challenge something I see repeated constantly in conversations about technology and older adults.

The assumption is that seniors struggle with technology because they lack the technical ability.

After building the Digital Confidence Centre and talking with hundreds of people in this demographic — I can tell you that's wrong.

Most seniors have the dexterity to use a touchscreen. They have the memory to recall steps they've been shown. They have the intelligence to evaluate new information.

What many of them lack is the belief that those skills apply to technology.

Somewhere along the way, a story got told — by media, by family members, by the tech industry itself — that digital tools belong to a younger generation. That if you didn't grow up with them, you're playing catch-up you'll never close.

That story is false. And it's doing real harm.

Low digital confidence correlates with social isolation. It limits access to healthcare information, banking services, government resources, and human connection.

Building confidence — not teaching features — has to be the goal of any digital literacy program worth its name.

The skill gap is smaller than you think. The confidence gap is enormous. And we can close it.
image_prompt: Older adult looking directly at camera with a confident smile, holding a tablet — strong, dignified, not patronising

text:
How accessibility and good UX are actually the same thing.

I used to think of accessibility as a checklist. Contrast ratios. Alt text. Screen reader compatibility.

All of those matter. But that framing misses something important.

Accessibility isn't a feature set. It's a design philosophy.

When you design for someone with low vision, you get better contrast for everyone in bright sunlight.

When you design for someone with motor difficulties, you get bigger touch targets for everyone using a phone with one hand.

When you design for someone who has low digital confidence, you get clearer language and more forgiving error states for every user who's ever felt confused by your product.

At the Digital Confidence Centre, we design primarily for adults in their 70s and 80s using iPads, often in varying light conditions, sometimes with reading glasses, always with real patience but finite tolerance for complexity.

And what we've found — consistently — is that the decisions we make for accessibility make the product better for everyone.

Accessibility isn't the extra effort at the end. It's the quality bar throughout.

If your product doesn't work well for your most challenged user, it doesn't work as well as it could for anyone.

Who is your hardest user to design for? And have you made them a priority?
image_prompt: Split comparison showing a cluttered app screen vs. the same content redesigned with clear typography, generous spacing, and high contrast

text:
19 modules. 167 pages. Zero budget. Here's what's possible when you have clarity of purpose.

I want to share some numbers.

The Digital Confidence Centre is a free, bilingual, fully accessible digital literacy platform for Canadian seniors.

19 modules. Covering everything from password safety to AI literacy to grocery delivery apps.
167 pages of content. Written in plain language, reviewed for accessibility, localised for Ontario.
Zero paid advertising. All organic reach through community partnerships and word of mouth.
Zero backend infrastructure costs. Static site. GitHub Pages. Cloudflare CDN. The whole thing runs for free.

None of this required a large team or a large budget.

It required clarity.

Clarity about who it was for. Clarity about what problem it was solving. Clarity about what 'done' looked like.

When you have that, a remarkable amount becomes possible with very little.

I'm not saying budget doesn't matter — it does, and there are real limits to what we can do without it.

But I've seen well-funded projects fail because they never got clear. And I've seen scrappy, purposeful projects do things no one expected.

Clarity is the rarest resource in product development. Not money. Not talent. Clarity.

What project would you build if you got brutally clear about what it was actually for?
image_prompt: Bold data graphic: '19 modules. 167 pages. Zero budget.' in large clean typography, strong blue and white palette

text:
What building for the least digitally confident users teaches you about good product design.

If you want a crash course in product fundamentals, try designing for someone who is actively afraid of breaking something.

When your user has low confidence, every design flaw is amplified. Ambiguous button labels become barriers. Unexpected state changes become panic. Error messages without recovery paths become proof that they were right to be afraid.

Building for seniors with low digital confidence has made me a better product thinker in ways that years of corporate product management didn't.

Here's what I've carried forward:

Clarity beats cleverness. Every time. If your label requires interpretation, it's wrong.

Every dead end needs a door. Whatever can go wrong, show the way back.

Confidence is cumulative. Small wins compound. Design for the first success, not the full feature set.

Language is UX. The words on a button are as important as its placement. Maybe more.

Don't assume — observe. What you think is intuitive almost certainly isn't for someone who doesn't share your context.

These aren't senior-specific principles. They're good product principles that become impossible to ignore when you're building for someone who has no patience for bad design.

The most unforgiving user makes you the most precise designer.

Who's the hardest user on your product right now?
image_prompt: Minimalist graphic showing a product design flowchart focused on user confidence, clean and professional

text:
The top 5 phone scams targeting Canadian seniors right now.

This list is based on data from the Canadian Anti-Fraud Centre and community reports from across Ontario.

Share this. It might protect someone you love.

1. The Grandparent Scam
A caller claims to be a grandchild in trouble — arrested, in an accident, or stranded abroad. They ask for emergency cash. They beg you not to tell anyone. This scam is emotionally devastating and financially serious. The rule: always hang up and call your grandchild directly on a number you already have.

2. The CRA Impersonation Scam
You owe back taxes. Your SIN has been compromised. A warrant is out for your arrest. None of this is how the CRA operates — but it sounds terrifying. The CRA does not demand immediate payment by gift card, wire transfer, or cryptocurrency. Ever.

3. The Bank Fraud Alert Scam
Your bank calls to say your account has been compromised. They need your card number to verify your identity. Real banks never ask for your PIN or full card number over the phone. Hang up and call the number on the back of your card.

4. The Tech Support Scam
A pop-up or call tells you your computer has a virus. They need remote access to fix it. Once in, they install actual malware or steal personal information. Legitimate tech companies do not call you unsolicited.

5. The Prize / Lottery Scam
Congratulations — you've won something. You just need to pay a small fee to release the prize. There is no prize. Stop there.

If something feels wrong, it probably is. Trust that feeling.

Save this post. Share it. Talk about it at the dinner table.

→ Report fraud: Canadian Anti-Fraud Centre 1-888-495-8501
image_prompt: Bold warning-style infographic listing 5 scam types, clean red and white design, easy to read on mobile

text:
One question that stops most phishing attacks.

Phishing emails and text messages are getting harder to spot. They look real. They use your bank's logo, your government's language, your carrier's tone.

But there's one question that cuts through almost all of it:

"Did I initiate this contact?"

If the answer is no — if you didn't ask for a password reset, didn't enter a contest, didn't request a call from your bank — then everything that follows should be treated with suspicion.

Real institutions don't reach out with urgency unless you triggered it.

Your bank doesn't email you out of nowhere saying your account is frozen. The CRA doesn't text you with a link to verify your identity. Apple doesn't call you to say your iCloud has been compromised.

They might communicate with you — but they do it through channels you're already logged in to, not through unexpected messages with links and phone numbers you've never seen.

The moment you feel pressure to act fast, that's the signal to slow down.

Write this on a sticky note if you need to: "Did I start this conversation?"

If not — pause. Call someone. Look it up independently.

That one question, asked consistently, stops most phishing attacks cold.

Share this with someone who needs to hear it.
image_prompt: Clean graphic with the question 'Did I initiate this contact?' in large bold text, simple blue and white design — shareable tip card

text:
"I'll never fall for that" is the most dangerous thing to think about scams.

I've heard this dozens of times in workshops:

"Those scams work on other people. I'm too smart for that."

And then, a few months later, I sometimes hear the rest of the story.

Here's what the research consistently shows: the people most confident they won't be scammed are statistically more vulnerable, not less.

Why?

Because confidence lowers vigilance. And vigilance is the only thing that actually protects you.

Scammers are professionals. They run emotional scripts that have been tested on thousands of people. They know how to sound like your bank, your grandchild, your government. They know how to create urgency that bypasses rational thinking.

This isn't about intelligence. Highly educated people get scammed. Financial professionals get scammed. Former law enforcement officers get scammed.

Because the vulnerability isn't in your brain. It's in your nervous system. When you're frightened or excited enough, clear thinking becomes much harder for everyone.

The protection isn't being smarter than the scammer. It's having a pause built in before you act.

The 3-second rule. The "did I initiate this" check. The habit of calling someone before sending anything.

Humility about your own vulnerability isn't weakness. It's the most effective protection you have.

Share this with the confident person in your life who needs to hear it.
image_prompt: Graphic with a thought bubble containing 'I'll never fall for that' with a red X through it — challenge the assumption visually

text:
What to do in the first 10 minutes after you think you've been scammed.

First: you are not stupid. This happens to careful, intelligent people every day.

Second: time matters. Here's what to do immediately.

MINUTES 1-2 — Stop all contact
Do not respond to any further messages or calls from the same source. If you gave them remote access to your device, unplug it from the internet immediately (turn off Wi-Fi, disconnect the cable).

MINUTES 3-4 — Protect your accounts
If you shared banking information, call your bank right now using the number on the back of your card. Not a number they gave you. The one on the card. Ask them to flag the account and stop any pending transfers.

MINUTES 5-6 — Change passwords
If you shared any login details, change those passwords on a different device if possible. Start with email — it's the master key to everything else.

MINUTES 7-8 — Write everything down
Date, time, what was said, what was shared, any phone numbers or email addresses involved. You'll need this for the report.

MINUTES 9-10 — Report it
Canadian Anti-Fraud Centre: 1-888-495-8501
Local police (non-emergency line)
Your provincial consumer protection office

Reporting matters even if you don't get the money back — it helps protect others.

Then: tell someone. Shame keeps scams secret. Secrecy lets them continue.

Save this post. You might need it or someone you know might.
image_prompt: Clean step-by-step infographic showing 10-minute action plan, urgent but calm design — green and blue tones

text:
The safest way to share passwords with family members.

This comes up constantly in our workshops. Older adults want trusted family members — a child, a sibling, a caregiver — to be able to access their accounts if something happens.

It's a completely reasonable need. Here's how to handle it safely.

Option 1 — A password manager with emergency access
Some password managers (like Bitwarden) allow you to designate an emergency contact who can request access. There's a built-in waiting period so you can deny the request if you're fine. This is the most secure option.

Option 2 — A sealed physical document
Write your critical account credentials on paper. Seal it in an envelope. Give it to your lawyer, or store it somewhere only the right person knows about — not a drawer anyone could access. Update it annually.

Option 3 — Supervised sharing sessions
Instead of sharing passwords, have the family member present while you log in. They observe — they don't store. This works well for regular account reviews.

What NOT to do:
— Don't text passwords to anyone, ever. Text messages can be read if a phone is stolen.
— Don't email passwords. Email is not as secure as it feels.
— Don't use the same password everywhere so 'one is enough to share.'

There's no perfect answer. But there is a thoughtful one.

Have you talked to your family about this? It's a more important conversation than most people have had.
image_prompt: Simple illustrated graphic showing three options as icons: password manager, sealed envelope, shared screen — clean and informative

text:
Why we recommend NOT using the same password manager your bank recommends.

This might seem counterintuitive. Your bank knows security, right?

Here's the issue.

When your bank recommends a password manager, they often recommend one because of a partnership or because it integrates well with their own products. That's not a bad reason — but it's not the same as recommending the most secure, most trustworthy option for your overall digital life.

Password managers hold the keys to everything. Every account, every login, potentially your email — which is the recovery address for everything else. The password manager you choose is one of the most consequential security decisions you'll make.

We recommend choosing independently based on:
— Independent security audits (look for managers that publish these)
— Open-source code (it can be verified by anyone)
— Zero-knowledge architecture (even the company can't see your passwords)
— Reputation over time, not just marketing

Bitwarden and 1Password consistently score well on these criteria. They're not perfect — nothing is — but they're chosen on security merit, not partnerships.

Your bank's recommendation might be fine. But verify it independently.

When it comes to the thing that protects everything else, do your own homework.

Have questions about which password manager to use? Drop them in the comments.
image_prompt: Graphic showing a padlock icon with 'Choose independently' text, professional blue and grey tones

text:
How AI is making phone scams more convincing — and what to watch for.

For years, you could spot a phone scam by the voice. An accent. Awkward phrasing. A script that felt rehearsed.

Those signals are disappearing.

AI voice cloning can now replicate a person's voice with as few as three seconds of audio. That means a scammer who finds a short video of your grandchild on social media — a birthday greeting, a school recital — has enough to make a call that sounds exactly like them.

"Grandma, I'm in trouble. I can't call Mom. Please don't tell anyone."

In your grandchild's voice.

This is the new baseline. And it requires a new kind of vigilance.

What to do:

1. Establish a family code word. Pick a word that only your immediate family knows. If someone calls claiming to be a family member in trouble, ask for the word. A real family member will know it. A scammer won't.

2. Always hang up and call back. Even if the voice sounds exactly right. Hang up and call the number you already have in your phone. If they're really in trouble, they'll answer.

3. Be suspicious of urgency + secrecy. Real emergencies don't usually come with instructions not to tell anyone. That combination is almost always a scam.

AI is a remarkable technology. It's also in the hands of people who will use it to steal from your family.

Talk about this at dinner. Share this post. The best defence is knowing it's happening.
image_prompt: Split image: phone screen showing an incoming call, with a visual hint of an AI waveform overlaid — warning but not alarmist

text:
The simple habit that protects most seniors from most online threats.

We teach 19 modules of digital safety at the Digital Confidence Centre.

If someone only has time for one thing — this is what I tell them.

Pause before you act on anything unexpected.

That's it.

Not a software tool. Not a subscription service. A habit.

An unexpected email asking you to verify your account → pause.
A pop-up saying your device has a virus → pause.
A phone call from someone saying you owe money → pause.
A text message with a link you didn't request → pause.

In that pause, you do three things:
1. Ask: did I initiate this?
2. Ask: does this feel right?
3. Call someone if you're unsure.

The scams that cost people the most money all have one thing in common: they work when you act before you think. Urgency is the mechanism. Removing urgency — even briefly — removes the mechanism.

You cannot out-clever every scam. The tactics change too fast. But you can build a pause into your responses to anything that surprises you online.

The pause is free. It requires no technical knowledge. And it prevents more harm than any software I've ever seen.

Share this with one person today.
image_prompt: Simple graphic with one word 'PAUSE' in large, calm typography, soft blue background — shareable and memorable

text:
What Canadian anti-fraud resources actually exist — and most people don't know about.

Canada has a remarkably good set of anti-fraud resources. Most people — including most seniors — have never heard of them.

Here's what exists:

Canadian Anti-Fraud Centre (CAFC)
The national hub for fraud reporting and information.
📞 1-888-495-8501
🌐 antifraudcentre-centreantifraude.ca

Phonebusters
The CAFC's original name — still referenced in some older resources. Same organisation.

Get Cyber Safe (Government of Canada)
Free online resources for individuals and families on digital safety.
🌐 getcybersafe.gc.ca

Consumer Protection Ontario
For scams involving Ontario-based businesses or services.
🌐 ontario.ca/consumerprotection
📞 1-800-889-9768

Seniors Canada
Federal resource hub including fraud prevention specifically for older adults.
🌐 seniorscanada.ca

Your Local Police Non-Emergency Line
Always worth reporting locally too — patterns in your community matter.

Credit Bureau Fraud Alerts
Equifax: 1-800-465-7166
TransUnion: 1-800-663-9980
Both offer fraud alerts that flag unusual activity on your credit file.

Knowing these numbers before you need them is the point.

Save this post. Print it out. Put it on the fridge.

And please share it — this information reaches far fewer people than it should.
image_prompt: Clean reference card graphic listing resources with phone numbers, maple leaf motif, designed to be saved or printed

text:
Why digital literacy is the best defence against scams — better than any software.

Software can block known threats.

Digital literacy handles everything else.

Here's what I mean:

Antivirus software catches malware that's already been identified. Spam filters catch email patterns that are already flagged. Two-factor authentication adds a layer, but only if you know how to use it and understand why.

Every software solution has the same limitation: it's reactive. It's built on what's already happened.

Scammers know this. It's why the best scams are social, not technical. They don't try to break your software. They call you on the phone and ask you to bypass it yourself.

Digital literacy is different because it's forward-looking. A person who understands how scams work, who recognises the patterns of urgency and secrecy, who knows where to look something up before acting — that person is protected against threats that don't exist yet.

That's not hypothetical. The AI voice cloning scams emerging now weren't in any threat database a year ago. But someone who'd been taught to pause and call back directly — they were already protected.

Software is a tool. Literacy is a capability.

Invest in both. But if you're choosing where to put most of your energy, choose the one that adapts.

What's your organisation doing on digital literacy this year?
image_prompt: Graphic comparing software shield (reactive) vs. human brain/education (proactive) — visual metaphor for literacy over tools

text:
What 20 years in corporate PM taught me that no MBA program covers.

I spent two decades in product management before stepping away to build independently.

In that time, I worked at companies with large budgets, established teams, and processes for the processes.

Here's what I learned that isn't in any curriculum:

Alignment is the job. Not strategy. Not roadmaps. Not frameworks. The actual job is getting people who have different information, different incentives, and different definitions of success to move in the same direction long enough for something to get built.

Stakeholders don't block projects — they protect priorities. When you understand what someone is actually protecting, the conversation changes entirely.

The best PMs I've ever worked with were remarkable listeners. Not in a passive way — in an active, analytical way. They heard what wasn't being said and built for the real problem, not the stated one.

Clarity is leadership. Not authority. Not seniority. The person in the room who can say 'here's what we're actually deciding' is the most powerful person in that room.

And finally: most product problems are people problems. The technical challenge is rarely the hard part.

None of this showed up in any course I took. All of it mattered more than anything that did.

What's the most important thing your career taught you that no one actually teaches?
image_prompt: Professional, thoughtful photo of someone in a meeting or looking at a whiteboard — real working environment, not staged

text:
The real reason I left Telus — and what happened next.

The version I used to tell in interviews was clean: I wanted to build something of my own. I wanted to work on problems that mattered to me directly.

That's true. But it's not the whole story.

The longer truth is that I had been building on other people's terms for long enough that I'd lost track of what my own terms even were.

So I stopped. Not dramatically. Not dramatically at all, actually. I just created some space to think.

And in that space, a strange thing happened. Instead of anxiously filling it with networking calls and job applications, I started building.

A digital literacy platform for seniors. An AI career coaching tool. A rental search system. A business diagnostic for small local businesses.

None of it was assigned. None of it had a budget. All of it had a clear answer to the question: who needs this?

I discovered that the skill set I'd spent 20 years developing in corporate environments didn't disappear when I left. It sharpened when I could apply it on my own terms.

I'm not anti-corporate. Some of the best experiences of my career were inside large organisations.

But I learned something important: I do my best work when I'm clear on the problem, free to design the solution, and accountable to the people I'm serving — not the process.

That's what happened next. I'm still figuring out what's after that.

And I'm okay with that.
image_prompt: Reflective scene of someone at a desk with a notebook and coffee, looking out a window — introspective but forward-looking

text:
What building for seniors teaches you about what everyone actually needs from technology.

I started the Digital Confidence Centre thinking I was building for a niche audience.

I ended up learning something universal.

Here's what seniors tell us they need:

Clear language. No jargon.
Patient design. Enough time to think.
Recovery paths. What do I do when it goes wrong?
Respect. Don't assume I'm less capable than I am.
Small wins. Show me I'm making progress.

Now tell me — which of those would any user NOT want?

The things that make technology work for a 78-year-old who's never owned a smartphone are the same things that make technology work for everyone else. We've just learned to accept their absence as normal.

We accept apps that punish errors instead of recovering from them.
We accept interfaces that assume you already know what to do.
We accept language designed for people who built the product.

Seniors don't accept these things. They just stop using the product.

And honestly? They're right.

Building for the most underserved user in the room doesn't constrain your product. It reveals what it should have been for everyone all along.

Who's the underserved user in your product's room?
image_prompt: Side-by-side showing a complex app vs. a clean, simple one — visual case for design that works for everyone

text:
On using AI to build things faster — and what speed costs you.

I've used AI tools extensively in my recent builds. Claude, primarily. The Digital Confidence Centre, the Career Coach tool, the apartment search system — all of them built with significant AI assistance.

And I want to be honest about something the 'AI makes you 10x more productive' narrative glosses over.

Speed is real. Absolutely real. Things that would have taken me weeks took days. The ability to draft, iterate, test, and refine at a pace that would have been impossible alone — that's genuine.

But speed has a cost.

The cost is judgment.

AI doesn't know when something is wrong if you don't know what right looks like. It doesn't have instincts about your users. It can't tell you when a feature is being built for a use case that doesn't exist.

Every tool I've built quickly, I've also had to slow down to review carefully. The speed of generation doesn't reduce the need for experienced judgement — it just concentrates that need at a different point in the process.

What changes is where your time goes. Less time generating. More time evaluating.

That shift is powerful if you have 20 years of product intuition behind the evaluation. It's risky if you don't.

AI amplifies the builder. It doesn't replace the thinking.

How are you using AI in your building process? I'm genuinely curious.

text:
Why I care more about the problem than the solution.

Early in my product management career, I got excited about solutions.

A feature that solved a thing. A workflow that made something faster. A design that felt elegant.

I still appreciate all of that. But what gets me out of bed now is the problem.

Specifically: the gap between what someone needs and what currently exists for them.

Seniors in Ontario who feel shut out of digital life because nobody built anything with them in mind — that's a problem.

Job seekers who can't get past ATS screening because they don't have access to coaching — that's a problem.

Small business owners who don't know what's holding them back because nobody's given them a clear diagnostic — that's a problem.

When you start with the problem and stay close to it — when you resist the urge to jump to the solution before you're sure you understand the problem — something happens.

You build things that actually help.

Not things that are impressive. Not things that win awards. Things that close a real gap for a real person.

I've built plenty of things in my career that were solutions looking for problems. They weren't bad work. But they didn't feel like this.

Problem-first is slower. It's less exciting in the early stages. It's harder to pitch to stakeholders.

And the things you end up building are better every time.

What problem are you closest to right now?
image_prompt: Whiteboard or notebook with 'What's the problem?' written prominently — genuine, working-environment feel

text:
The two questions I ask before every project.

I've run a lot of projects. Inside large organisations and on my own. With teams and solo.

I've tried many frameworks, templates, and kickoff rituals over the years.

Most of them got replaced. Two questions survived everything.

Question 1: Who is this for, specifically?

Not 'seniors.' Not 'SMEs.' Not 'job seekers.' A specific person or a small group of specific people with a shared, concrete need. If I can't describe them in one sentence, I don't know enough yet.

Question 2: What changes for them if this works?

Not 'they'll have better access to information.' Specifically: what does Tuesday morning look like for them after this exists that's different from Tuesday morning now?

If I can answer both questions clearly, the project has a foundation.

If I can't — no amount of planning will make up for the missing clarity.

These questions seem obvious. They are obvious. And yet in my experience, the majority of projects that struggled or failed could be traced back to fuzzy answers to one or both of them.

'We're building for everyone' is an answer that means nothing.
'It will improve their experience' doesn't tell you if you've succeeded.

Start with specificity. It's the only path to something that actually lands.

What do you ask before starting a new project?

text:
What I've learned about getting unstuck when you're building alone.

Building independently is different from building inside an organisation in one particular way that nobody warns you about.

There's no one to ask.

Not rhetorically. Literally. The decisions that in a corporate environment would spark a meeting, a Slack thread, or a whiteboard session — when you're building alone, they just sit there until you make them.

I've learned some things about getting through those moments.

Write the problem out loud. The act of writing a decision down — fully, in complete sentences — often reveals the answer. Or at least clarifies what's actually unclear.

Change the question. 'What should I build?' is almost never the stuck question. The stuck question is usually 'who is this actually for' or 'what does success look like.' Find the question behind the question.

Build something small to test the assumption. When I'm unsure whether an approach is right, the fastest path through is often to make a tiny version and see how it feels. Not to think about it more.

Talk to one real person. Not a focus group. Not a survey. One person who experiences the problem you're solving. That conversation reorients everything.

The resistance that makes you feel stuck is almost always information. It's telling you something about the decision that you haven't yet understood.

What do you do when you hit a wall mid-project?

text:
On the difference between features and value.

Features are what the product does.

Value is what changes for the person using it.

These are not the same thing. And confusing them is the most common mistake I see in product development.

'We've added biometric login' — that's a feature.
'You'll never have to remember a password again' — that's a value statement.

'The platform now includes 17 modules' — feature.
'You can go from overwhelmed by your phone to confident in two hours' — value.

The difference matters because users don't buy features. They buy the change they want for themselves.

When I was building the Digital Confidence Centre, I had to fight the urge to lead with what it contained. The module count, the page count, the language options.

What mattered to our users wasn't any of that. What mattered was: will I feel less scared? Will I be able to do this on my own? Will I stop feeling left behind?

Features answer the question 'what does this do?'
Value answers 'what does this do for me?'

If your product pitch is mostly features, try translating each one into the human outcome it creates. Not what the feature is — what it gives the person.

Sometimes that translation reveals the feature isn't actually delivering value at all.

That's useful to know before you build it.

text:
Why the best product managers are the ones who say no the most.

This is counterintuitive. PMs are often evaluated on what they ship. On features completed. On roadmap delivered.

But the best product managers I've known — and the periods where I've done my best work — aren't characterised by how much got built.

They're characterised by the quality of what didn't.

Every feature you don't build is:
— Technical debt you're not taking on
— User confusion you're preventing
— Maintenance burden you're avoiding
— Focus you're protecting

Saying no isn't the absence of contribution. It's often the highest-leverage contribution a PM can make.

But it's hard. Because every feature request comes from a person with a real reason. A stakeholder protecting a priority. A user with a genuine need. A executive with a strategic bet.

Saying no means making a judgement that this request, however reasonable, is not the right use of the team's limited capacity right now.

That judgement requires clarity about what the product is actually for. Which requires a clear definition of the user and the problem. Which requires doing the thinking that most organisations skip because they're busy building.

The best PMs say no constantly. Politely, thoughtfully, with a clear explanation.

And the products they build are better for it.

What's the hardest 'no' you've ever delivered on a product?

text:
What I'd tell someone 20 years earlier starting in product management.

I've been thinking about this a lot lately.

If I could sit across from the version of me who was just starting out — ambitious, somewhat anxious, very confident about the wrong things — here's what I'd say.

The frameworks don't matter as much as you think. Learn them. Use them. Then forget about impressing anyone with them. The frameworks are vocabulary. The insight is still yours to develop.

Get close to the user as fast as possible. Not data about the user. The user. Sit with them. Watch them struggle. Ask them what they were hoping for. Nothing calibrates you like that.

Be the person who makes things clear. In meetings, in documents, in conversations. Clarity is the rarest skill in product and the most valuable.

Say no earlier. You'll spend a lot of time early in your career trying to say yes to everything to prove you're a team player. You'll learn — eventually — that protecting the team from the wrong work is the most valuable thing you can do.

The best product work is invisible. If you need people to know it was your call, it wasn't the right call.

And lastly: the products you're most proud of will be the ones you built for someone specific, with a clear problem in mind, where you stayed close to the truth the whole way through.

Everything else is practice.

What would you tell your earlier self starting out?
